title: 17  Quantum key distribution (QKD) and BB84 in qg space
text:
17.1 From the base: four readings and the image of the sphere
Chapter 16 left BB84’s QBER on the side of what qang reads: it is the probability of a qubit, and the security threshold sits in the middle of the scale, at 780 m-qg. This chapter opens it up. The QBER is a single number, and a real link has four: each state Alice sends reaches Bob with its own error probability. On the scale of Chapter 1 those four readings say where the image of the Bloch sphere ended up after the channel, and the shape of that image tells apart two causes the QBER confuses: a memory that degrades and an eavesdropper who intercepts. The chapter says how far that distinction goes, with finite key blocks, with subtler attacks and with trapped-ion noise, and where it does not go.
In BB84 Alice sends \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\) (Z basis) or \(|+\rangle\) or \(|-\rangle\) (X basis); the qubit waits in a memory or travels through a channel, and Bob measures. After sifting only the rounds in which Bob measured in Alice’s basis remain. For each sent state, Bob’s reading in its own basis is a reading of Chapter 1:
\[
m(0)=1000\,(1-2e_{0\to1}),\qquad m(1)=-1000\,(1-2e_{1\to0}),
\]
and likewise for \(|\pm\rangle\) in X. An ideal channel gives \(\pm1000\). A real channel maps the sphere to an ellipsoid, and in each basis the two readings give its centre and its semi-axis:
\[
c_Z=\frac{m(0)+m(1)}{2},\qquad r_Z=\frac{m(0)-m(1)}{2},\qquad Q_Z=\frac{1}{2}\Big(1-\frac{r_Z}{1000}\Big).
\]
The QBER is exactly the semi-axis, with no approximation. The index’s formula, \(Q=(1-|qg|)/2\), is the symmetric case, in which the two readings of a basis have the same modulus; in general \(|m(0)|\neq|m(1)|\), and the difference is the centre. The asymmetry \(A_Z=qg(0)+qg(1)\) of the notes (§40) is \(2c_Z\): the T1 witness of §24.
The two causes move the image in different directions. T1 relaxation of the memory is affine, \(z\mapsto(1-\gamma)z+\gamma\): it leaves \(|0\rangle\) at the pole and lifts \(|1\rangle\), so that \(c_Z\) goes up and \(r_Z\) goes down by the same amount. An eavesdropper who intercepts and resends a fraction \(f\) of the qubits, measuring in a random basis, shrinks the sphere before the memory: \(r_Z\) goes down and \(c_Z\) does not move, exactly, because the affine memory puts the centre at a place that depends only on \(\gamma\). In the \((c_Z,r_Z)\) plane the drift is a line of slope \(-1\) and the eavesdropper a vertical (Figure 17.1, left).
The channel of the notes: a memory with \(\gamma_0=0.02\) (T1), dephasing \(p_0=0.01\) and an asymmetric detector (\(e_{01}=0.005\), \(e_{10}=0.01\), calibrated as in §31).
In a window of \(N\) compared bits, \(N/4\) per state, the shot noise of \(c_Z\) and of \(r_Z\) is 16.4, 8.2 and 3.7 m-qg for \(N=500\), 2000 and 10,000. The memory going from \(\gamma=0.02\) to \(0.04\) moves the centre by 19.7 m-qg: with 2000 bits, 2.4 standard deviations.

Three things can be read from the table.

Detection is the same; false alarms are not. The qg monitor catches the naive eavesdropper as well as the QBER monitor, at every \(N\) and \(f\), within the sampling spread. When the memory degrades, the QBER monitor fires in 48% and 96% of windows (\(N=2000\)) and the qg monitor stays at 0.9% and 0.6%, at the baseline level. The reduction in false alarms holds for T1 drift, which is in the qg monitor’s model, and not for any degradation whatsoever.
The price, by design. An eavesdropper who couples the qubit to her ancilla through an amplitude-damping interaction produces exactly the counts of a T1 drift, because in the \((c_Z,r_Z)\) plane she runs along the same line. The qg monitor misses her (0.6%, the same figure as the drift, because the counts are identical), and the QBER monitor does not (96%). The two are complementary: QBER says “something changed”; qg says “symmetric (attack-like)” or “T1-like (drift, or an eavesdropper hiding as one)”.
No security gain. The secret fraction falls the same way in both cases (0.720 → 0.567 with drift to 0.06; 0.720 → 0.594 with \(f=0.05\)). A security proof must charge every error to Eve, and the qg reading does not change that.

The setting is a link with matter qubits, or an on-chip demonstration, where the qubit waits with T1 and T2 before Bob measures. In a photon-polarization link the noise is nearly unital, the centre does not move, and the distinction does not exist.

17.3 Finite blocks
A real link cuts the key into blocks. The notes (§43) use the finite-key bound of Tomamichel, Lim, Gisin and Renner (Nat. Commun. 3, 634, 2012) on the same channel:
\[
\ell=n\big[1-h(Q_{\text{tol}}+\mu)\big]-1.1\,n\,h(Q_Z)-\log_2\frac{2}{\varepsilon_{\text{sec}}^2\varepsilon_{\text{cor}}},\qquad
\mu=\sqrt{\frac{n+k}{nk}\,\frac{k+1}{k}\,\ln\frac{2}{\varepsilon_{\text{sec}}}},
\]

Partial cloning is caught. The optimal cloner comes out as an attack in every block, like intercepting with \(f=4D\), because Bob sees the same counts. What no error statistic shows is that the cloner gives Eve more information per error; the key rate, which charges every error to Eve, already accounts for it.
The two-family model had a false alarm. Without the dephasing family, T2 drift raised the attack flag in 7.5% and 27% of blocks. With the family, the false alarm drops to 0.7–2% and the verdict is T2 in every block.
A second blind spot, by construction. A Z-only intercept shrinks only the X axis, like T2: it comes out as T2 drift and not as an attack. It is the twin of the T1-mimicking attack: an eavesdropper hiding in the error type the hardware makes by itself. An X-only intercept has no natural twin, and is always caught.
Mixtures are resolved: T2 drift plus a cloner raises both flags.

title: 17  Quantum key distribution (QKD) and BB84 in qg space
text:
17.5 On IonQ’s noisy simulator
So far the channel was analytic. In the notes (§44) every part of BB84 is a circuit run on the aria-1 and forte-1 noise models of IonQ’s simulator (free; nothing was sent to a QPU), and the model behind the flags is fitted, not given.

The memory is amplitude damping built with an ancilla, CRY\((2\arcsin\sqrt\gamma)\) followed by CX, with a healthy \(\gamma_0=0.02\) and drifts from 0.03 to 0.06.
Eve measures and resends (CX to her ancilla in Z, H·CX·H in X), never reading the ancilla; a fraction \(f\) of the rounds is taken from those circuits.
The runs: 32 circuits in native gates, 4 copies of each (12 qubits), 2000 shots, 4 repetitions per noise model. Each copy is a block of \(n=k=4000\) bits.
The flag model is the joint one (\(\gamma\), \(f\)) plus two symmetric device flip rates, \(\varepsilon_Z\) and \(\varepsilon_X\), fitted leaving out each repetition, with thresholds from a parametric bootstrap at 1%.

The device adds a nearly symmetric error of 2.3–2.4% per bit (aria-1) and 2.8–3.1% (forte-1), mostly from the two MS gates of the memory circuit. On the image of the sphere that is a shrinking, not a shift. The designed healthy memory gives \(c_Z=20\), \(r_Z=980\) and \(r_X=990\) m-qg; the simulator gives \(c_Z=18.5\) and \(20.6\) m-qg (aria-1, forte-1), with the semi-axes 46–62 m-qg lower; with \(\gamma=0.06\) the centre rises to 60.5 and 56.5 m-qg, where the design says 60. The device noise leaves the centre in place, which is what the T1 witness needs to keep working. The fit recovers the designed \(\gamma_0\) (0.020–0.0225) in every fold.

title: 17  Quantum key distribution (QKD) and BB84 in qg space
text:
17.9 Summary

In BB84 each sent state has its reading; in each basis, the two readings give the centre and the semi-axis of the image of the sphere, and the QBER is exactly the semi-axis: \(Q=(1-r/1000)/2\).
T1 drift shifts the centre and shrinks by the same amount; an intercepting eavesdropper shrinks without moving the centre. Hence the qg monitor stays quiet under drift (0.6–0.9% against 48–96%) and sees the eavesdropper as well as the QBER does.
By construction, an eavesdropper who mimics T1, or who intercepts only in Z (and looks like T2), comes out as drift.
With finite blocks of \(10^5\) bits the attribution is nearly exact, at no key cost, and an attack hidden under drift raises both flags; IonQ’s simulator confirms it with 4000-bit blocks, in part.
The secret key does not grow: the qg reading is a diagnostic, not security.

title: 18  Certified quantum random numbers (QRNG) and channel auditing
text:
18.1 From the base: output and privacy are different readings
A one-qubit quantum random number generator (QRNG) is the simplest experiment in the book: prepare \(|+\rangle\), measure in Z, write down the bit. The result is a fair coin, and that is what the usual analysis measures. But a fair coin is not the same as a private coin. If the qubit lost coherence, the output still comes out 50/50, and yet someone holding the environment can know every bit in advance. This chapter reads that difference on the scale of Chapter 1. The output lives in one reading and privacy in the other two, and what the adversary knows is one more reading: the one the state lacks to reach the sphere. The chapter adds the readout calibration needed to avoid overestimating, and the same certifier against a designed leak on IonQ’s simulator.
The source qubit has three readings, \(m_X\), \(m_Y\) and \(m_Z\). The QRNG output is the measurement in Z, and the usual analysis looks only at its bias: with \(p_0=(1000+m_Z)/2000\) it certifies
\[
H_{\text{naive}}=-\log_2\max(p_0,p_1)=-\log_2\frac{1000+|m_Z|}{2000}
\]
bits per shot, 1 bit when \(m_Z=0\). But \(m_Z=0\) is given by \(|+\rangle\) and by the completely mixed state alike, and in the second case nothing is private: the environment holds the other half of the purification and knows what came out.
With a trusted measurement and an adversary (Eve) holding the purification, Eve’s two conditional states are pure, and their overlap depends only on the transverse radius \(r_\perp=\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2}\). By Helstrom, her guessing probability is (notes, §41)
\[
P_{\text{guess}}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-r_\perp^2}}{2},\qquad H_{\min}(Z|E)=-\log_2 P_{\text{guess}}.
\]
On the scale of Chapter 1, that probability is one more reading. Its value in m-qg is
\[
m_E=1000\sqrt{1-r_\perp^2}=\sqrt{1000^2-m_X^2-m_Y^2},
\]
what the transverse radius lacks to reach the sphere, and its qang angle is \(\arcsin r_\perp\). The formula does not depend on \(m_Z\). A pure state on the equator has \(m_\perp=1000\) and leaves Eve at \(m_E=0\): she guesses with probability 1/2, and the bit is private. A state that lost coherence has \(m_\perp<1000\), and the length it lost is what Eve knows (Figure 18.1, left).
The shape of the formula has a practical consequence. Ten m-qg less of transverse radius, from 1000 to 990, give Eve 141 m-qg and take 0.19 bits per shot from the source. It is the pole of Chapter 1 seen from the other side: near \(m_\perp=1000\), the square root has infinite slope.

section: 18.4 Readout calibration: temperature or detector error
text:
18.4 Readout calibration: temperature or detector error
The calibrated certifier divides by the readout scale factor \(b\), and the question is where \(b\) comes from. On the scale of Chapter 1 the readout is affine (notes, §31):
\[
m_{\text{measured}}=1000\,a+b\,m,\qquad a=e_{10}-e_{01},\quad b=1-e_{01}-e_{10}.
\]
A real qubit starts with thermal population \(p\), that is with \(m_{\text{eq}}=1000(1-2p)=1000\tanh(hf/2k_BT_{\text{eff}})\). The standard calibration measures “\(|0\rangle\)” and “\(|1\rangle\)”, which are really the thermal state and X on it: two readings for three unknowns (\(a\), \(b\), \(m_{\text{eq}}\)). It assumes \(m_{\text{eq}}=1000\) and charges the thermal population to the readout: it reports \(e_{01}+p\,b\) and \(e_{10}+p\,b\), exactly.

18.5 On IonQ’s noisy simulator, with a leak
In the notes (§42) the leak is real: an ion \(q\) is the source and a second ion \(e\) plays the environment. An MS\((0,0,\theta)\) interaction lets \(e\) learn the X value of \(q\), and the output is read in X. It is still a fair coin, but the private randomness falls to the formula above with \(r=|\cos2\pi\theta|\) (X and Z exchanged). Test rounds measure ±Z and ±Y, and two circuits calibrate the readout. title: 18  Certified quantum random numbers (QRNG) and channel auditing
text:
18.9 Summary

The output of a one-qubit QRNG is the reading \(m_Z\); its privacy is the transverse radius \(m_\perp\). What an adversary holding the purification knows is one more reading, \(m_E=\sqrt{1000^2-m_\perp^2}\).
The output-bias analysis certifies almost 1 bit per shot even when the state is almost mixed: unsafe in 100% of runs with dephasing or thermal mixing. The qg estimator with ± pairs is safe in all of them.
Near the pole certification is expensive: 10 m-qg of radius are worth 0.19 bits, and a perfect source gives 0.69 certified bits with \(10^4\) rounds and 0.89 with \(10^6\).
The standard calibration reads temperature as readout error, and using it makes the certifier unsafe. The §31 protocol separates them and recovers 10–50% of bits.
On IonQ’s simulator, with a designed leak, the naive estimator does not see it and the qg one is safe in every cell.

title: 19  Quantum batteries and networks
text:
19.1 From the base: three distances between readings
A quantum battery is a system that stores energy to deliver it later as work. The smallest one is a qubit with \(H=\omega|1\rangle\langle1|\): charging it means bringing it towards \(|1\rangle\), and discharging it means returning it to \(|0\rangle\) with a unitary operation. The practical question is not how much energy the qubit has, but how much can be taken out, which is its ergotropy. This chapter reads it on the scale of Chapter 1. Energy, ergotropy and the part nobody can take out are three distances between readings. With that, the chapter answers how to charge a battery that will wait with T1 and T2, how much it costs to certify its charge from shots, and where the charge of a qubit register sits when it lives in the correlations. The last section turns to networks: a Bell pair stored in two memories is another thing stored with T1 and T2, and its useful time is read the same way.
A qubit with readings \((m_X,m_Y,m_Z)\) and radius \(m_r=\sqrt{m_X^2+m_Y^2+m_Z^2}\) has energy \(\omega(1000-m_Z)/2000\): the distance of its Z reading from the north pole, which is the ground state. Its ergotropy, the maximum work a unitary operation extracts, is (notes, §56)
\[
W=\omega\,\frac{m_r-m_Z}{2000},
\]
and what is left unextracted, the energy of the passive state, is \(\omega(1000-m_r)/2000\). The energy splits between how far the state sits below the top of its own sphere, \(m_r-m_Z\), and how much radius the sphere lost, \(1000-m_r\). A unitary rotates the state without changing its radius, so the best it can do is bring it to the top of its sphere, \(m_Z=m_r\). The part lost to mixing is out of reach of any unitary.
For a pure state, \(m_r=1000\) and \(W=\omega\sin^2(\theta/2)=\omega\,p_1\): the ergotropy is the probability equation of Chapter 1, with the qang angle as the charging angle (checked to \(2\cdot10^{-16}\)). The notes also split \(W=W_{\text{inc}}+W_{\text{coh}}\), with \(W_{\text{inc}}=\omega\max(0,-qg_Z)\) (population inversion) and \(W_{\text{coh}}=\tfrac{\omega}{2}(r-|qg_Z|)\) (coherence). The formulas match the general eigenvalue expression to \(3\cdot10^{-16}\) on 200 random states.
The last row is a passive battery: it has almost half a unit of energy and delivers nothing, because it sits at the top of its sphere (\(m_Z=m_r\)). This happens to every inverted battery when its Z reading crosses the equator upwards.

19.2 Storage with T1 and T2: inversion dies at the equator
A battery charged at angle \(\theta\) ages as
\[
m_Z(t)=1000\big[1-(1-\cos\theta)\,e^{-t/T_1}\big],\qquad m_\perp(t)=1000\sin\theta\,e^{-t/T_2}.
\]
The inverted battery (\(\theta=\pi\)) has no coherence and stores only inversion: \(m_Z=1000(1-2e^{-t/T_1})\), which crosses the equator at \(t=T_1\ln2\). There its ergotropy is zero, and it does not come back. A tilted battery stores less at first, but its coherence keeps it below the top of its sphere after the crossing, as long as \(T_2\) allows.

Ergotropy is estimated from shots on the three axes, and the formula has a trap. The estimated radius comes out inflated, because the noise of the three axes adds in quadrature: \(E[\hat r^2]=r^2+3\sigma^2\). section: 19.4 Registers: charge locked in the correlations
text:
19.4 Registers: charge locked in the correlations
In a register of qubits the charge can live in the correlations. The notes compare two batteries of 4 qubits with 2 excitations, both with energy \(2\omega\), aged with local noise (\(T_2=T_1\)):

the Dicke state \(D(4,2)\), the even superposition of the six registers with two ones;
a product of four qubits on the equator, with the same energy.

Read qubit by qubit, they are opposites. In the Dicke state each qubit reads \((m_X,m_Y,m_Z)=(0,0,0)\): local radius zero, the centre of the sphere, a passive qubit. In the product each qubit reads \((1000,0,0)\): radius 1000, ergotropy \(\omega/2\). Yet the mean Z reading of the register is identical in both at all times (0, 95, 259, 503 and 777 m-qg for \(t=0\), 0.1, 0.3, 0.7 and 1.5 \(T_1\)), and does not tell them apart.

The Dicke charge is locked. All of it is extractable with a global operation, and none with one-qubit operations: the sum of the local ergotropies is zero. The product’s charge is all local.
The local radius tells them apart; the mean reading does not. The sum of the local ergotropies, which comes from the three readings of each qubit, separates one battery from the other.
Locked charge is more fragile under local noise: 0.71 against \(1.05\,\omega\) at \(0.3\,T_1\), and 0.05 against \(0.41\,\omega\) at \(0.7\,T_1\).

Local radius zero is not new in the book. It is what the qubits of a Bell pair in a network read (Chapter 12, §57), and the counting qubits of Shor with \(N=21\) before the QFT (Chapter 16). In all three cases what matters is in the correlations, and a one-qubit reading can only say that it is not in that qubit.

text:
19.5 Networks: a Bell pair stored in two memories
A quantum network also stores something in memories with T1 and T2: the Bell pairs it distributes among its nodes. Chapter 12 read a pair in qg (three correlators and two local biases) and used that reading to choose how to distil it. The question of this section is still open, and it is the battery’s question: how long a pair can wait in memory before it is no longer useful. For \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) with both halves stored for a time \(t\), the readings have closed forms (notes, §57; they match the density matrix to \(5\cdot10^{-16}\)):
\[
c_x=-c_y=e^{-2t/T_2},\qquad c_z=1-2g+2g^2,\qquad m_A=m_B=1000\,g,\qquad g=1-e^{-t/T_1}.
\]
The local biases \(m_A\) and \(m_B\) rise from zero: it is the T1 witness on a shared pair, the same reading that shifted the centre of the image of the sphere in BB84 (Chapter 17). The pair is good for a BBM92 key while \(1-h(Q_X)-h(Q_Z)>0\), with \(Q_X=(1-c_x)/2\) and \(Q_Z=(1-c_z)/2\).

A pair lasts much less than a battery. One distillation round almost doubles the useful time when T1 limits it (0.184 → 0.395 at \(T_2=2T_1\)). It costs half the pairs, so with fresh pairs it lowers the key per input pair. Distil only after the crossover in the last row, and that crossover is read from the aged correlators.

title: 19  Quantum batteries and networks
text:
19.6 What remains open
Everything is exact or simulated: there is no hardware run. Missing are a real battery charged at different angles on a device with \(T_2\approx T_1\), where the charging rule can be tested, and the preparation of a Dicke \(D(4,2)\) with a measurement of its local ergotropy. On the network side, distillation is computed on the twirled (Bell-diagonal) state with perfect local gates, and the cutoff assumes equal memories at the two nodes.

title: 19  Quantum batteries and networks
text:
19.9 Summary

The energy of a qubit splits between the extractable part, \((m_r-m_Z)/2000\), and the part locked by mixing, \((1000-m_r)/2000\); for a pure state the ergotropy is the probability equation of Chapter 1, \(\omega\,p_1\).
An inverted battery dies when its Z reading crosses the equator, at \(t=T_1\ln2\). A tilted battery keeps charge after that if \(T_2\) is comparable to \(T_1\), and the charging rule has a closed crossover: \(\ln(4/3)\) for \(T_2=2T_1\), \(\ln(3/2)\) for \(T_2=T_1\).
The plug-in estimate of the ergotropy overestimates, and reports charge in a passive battery in almost every run; the 3σ bound is safe but expensive.
In a Dicke register all the charge is in the correlations: each qubit reads the centre of the sphere, the sum of the local ergotropies is zero, and the mean reading does not tell it apart from a product with the same energy.
A stored Bell pair gives key only up to \(0.05\)–\(0.18\,T_1\), much less than a battery; one distillation round almost doubles that time, and pays only after a crossover read from the correlators.

title: 20  Weight-conserving quantum neural networks (WeightQNN)
text:
20.1 From the base: a sector and its readings
Part VII is about quantum machine learning, and it starts with the network that fits the base of Chapter 1 best. A quantum neural network (QNN) that conserves the Hamming weight (the number of ones in the register) lives in a fixed sector, and that has two consequences. The first is good: the qg filter, which discards the shots that left the sector, makes the readout exact under T1 relaxation. The second is honest: such a network can be simulated on an ordinary computer, and cannot give a quantum advantage. This chapter reads the network in m-qg, checks its structural properties with code, and summarises the classification experiments of the notes (§75–§114), all with predictions committed before running, with and without qang.
The RBS gate (reconfigurable beam splitter) rotates the pair \(|01\rangle,|10\rangle\) by an angle \(\theta\) and leaves \(|00\rangle\) and \(|11\rangle\) alone: it is a Givens rotation, and it does not change the number of ones. In the weight-1 sector of \(n\) qubits the state is a unit vector \(u\in\mathbb R^n\), a layer of RBS gates is an orthogonal matrix, and each qubit has the reading of Chapter 1:
\[
m_Z(q)=1000\,(1-2u_q^2),
\]
because \(u_q^2\) is the probability that the excitation is on qubit \(q\). The notes’ network E (§76) loads the data as amplitudes, \(v=(x_1,\dots,x_4,1)/|(x,1)|\) on 5 qubits (the constant keeps the norm of \(x\)), applies 3 layers of RBS gates (9 sublayers, 15 parameters) and reads \(z=\sum_q c_q\,qg_Z(q)+b\). Network W does the same in the weight-2 sector.
The filter under T1. T1 relaxation takes a weight-\(k\) state to weight \(k-1\) and, if every qubit has the same T1, damps all weight-\(k\) amplitudes by the same factor. Keeping only the weight-\(k\) shots then returns the noiseless distribution, exactly, for any strength (notes, §76 F1 and §78 F4). The price is known before running: the filter keeps a fraction \(K=(1-\gamma)^{k\,d}\) of the shots, with \(d\) the number of sublayers, whatever the data or the parameters (§77).
On the scale of Chapter 1 one sees what the noise does without the filter. A shot that decayed has one fewer one, and its qubits read \(+1000\): raw readings drift towards the north pole. In the example of Figure 20.1 (weight 2, dual encoding), the five noiseless readings lie between 157 and 260 m-qg, the raw ones under T1 between 543 and 664, and the filtered ones return exactly to 157–260. The filter does not correct what does not change the weight: unequal T1 and dephasing leave biases of 30 to 90 m-qg.

The pair product distorts the data: its information ceiling, measured with a regression on all products of amplitudes, is 2.4 points lower. With the dual encoding, which puts \(v\) on the ring of pairs and \(u=(x^2,1)/|(x^2,1)|\) on the chords and covers all 10 weight-2 states, and with the \(qg_{ZZ}\) readout, weight 2 reaches weight 1: 0.947 = 0.947 (§90). Its gain with qang under T1 is 14 to 20 points, against 3 at weight 1.

At weight 1 the five \(m_Z\) readings already determine the whole distribution, and the correlations add nothing. At weight 2 the five readings see only 5 of the 10 directions, and the correlations \(qg_{ZZ}=\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle\) are needed. But rank was not the cause of the gap: with the pair encoding, adding \(qg_{ZZ}\) changed nothing (§81). Both things were needed together, an encoding that does not distort and a full-rank readout (§90).
The shots that decayed. In §81 there was one case against qang: with the pair encoding, the \(qg_{ZZ}\) readout and training under T1, the network without the filter scored 1.2 points more [0.4, 2.0], because the decayed shots still say where the excitations were. The two-channel readout (§95), which gives the classifier the filtered and the raw readings together, recovered nothing, and with 60 new runs the effect dropped to +0.5 [−0.7, 1.6] (§101). No readout trained under T1 beat the filter significantly, and with the simple readout the filter was better by 0.6 points [0.1, 1.0].

title: 20  Weight-conserving quantum neural networks (WeightQNN)
text:
20.4 Classical simulability: no quantum advantage
In the weight-1 sector the whole network is an \(n\times n\) orthogonal matrix \(O\). With \(u=Ov\),
\[
z=\sum_q c_q\,(1-2u_q^2)+b,
\]
a quadratic classifier in \(v\) that is computed in \(O(n^2)\) (§76 F2). The chapter’s script checks it: the network’s output and the quadratic twin’s agree to \(9\cdot10^{-16}\). At weight \(k\) the sector has dimension \(\binom nk\), and the network stays simulable as long as that number is manageable. That is why the notes say it plainly: on real data, the best classical model ties or beats the best QNN (§75: RBF-SVM 0.963 against 0.933 on digits), and a well-regularised quadratic twin sits within 0.3–1.6 points of E (§76). What these networks offer is robustness on noisy hardware, not quantum advantage.

text:
20.5 Scaling and multiclass
With 5, 6 and 8 qubits and a fixed depth of 9 sublayers (§111), the filter keeps every network at its noiseless accuracy. Without it, the weight-1 loss stays at 3.1–3.4 points, but the weight-2 loss grows from 8.7 to 26.0 points: an 8-qubit weight-2 network falls from 0.965 to 0.705 (Figure 20.2, left). Training under the noise still catches up with the filter (within 0.9 points in every cell).
In the multiclass version each qubit is a class (qang.qml.MultiClassQNN, §110 and §114). With 8 qubits and 3, 5 and 8 classes of digits, the filter keeps every model exactly at its noiseless accuracy; without it, the linear-head readout loses 0.7, 15.9 and 11.1 points. Unlike at 5 qubits, training under the noise no longer fully catches up: it stays 2–3 points behind with 5 and 8 classes.

Right: gradient of one qubit’s \(qg_Z\) with respect to the first angle in a three-qubit PennyLane circuit with Givens gates and amplitude damping (\(\gamma=0.08\)); the filtered gradient matches the noiseless one, and the raw one is the noiseless one times the kept fraction.

section: 20.6 Training under noise or with the filter
text:
20.6 Training under noise or with the filter
If the filtered readout under T1 is the noiseless one for every parameter, so are the loss and every gradient. That is why training under T1 with the filter gives exactly the parameters of noiseless training (§77 F3: to \(5\cdot10^{-9}\) after 120 Adam steps). The script checks it in PennyLane, with Givens gates (SingleExcitation) and amplitude damping on default.mixed: the gradient of the filtered readout matches that of the noiseless circuit to \(10^{-16}\), and the gradient of the raw readout is the noiseless one multiplied by \(K=0.716393=(1-\gamma)^4\), component by component (Figure 20.2, right). At weight 1 the raw gradient is \(K\) times smaller; with many qubits the sector itself flattens the gradient (§112), with or without the filter.

section: 20.7 The ecosystem: Qiskit, qiskit-machine-learning and PennyLane
text:
20.7 The ecosystem: Qiskit, qiskit-machine-learning and PennyLane
The network does not live in NumPy only. The notes take it to three environments:

Qiskit. qang.interop reads the qg readings from a SamplerV2, and writes the filtered readout as a ratio of two diagonal observables, \(\langle P_wZ_i\rangle/\langle P_w\rangle\), for an EstimatorV2 (§131). qang.ibm.qnn_template writes the weight-1 network as one parameterised circuit of native XX+YY gates and sends a whole test set in one job (§139).
qiskit-machine-learning. qang.qiskit_ml.qang_sampler_qnn turns the network into a SamplerQNN (§140). The notes found that qiskit-machine-learning 0.9.1 reads the measured bits at the physical positions of the layout, so a circuit measured before transpilation reads every shot as 0; qang transpiles by itself and drops the layout.
PennyLane. qang.pennylane_gate.filtered_qg_z acts on qml.probs() with qml.math, so the filtered readout is differentiable and can be the loss of a training loop (§131). Checking it for this chapter turned up a problem in PennyLane 0.45.1: on default.mixed, the backprop mode returns NaN for the jacobian of qml.probs through SingleExcitation (with RY it works, and on default.qubit too). The parameter-shift rule gives the right value.

qml.math also covers PennyLane’s JAX interface, but JAX is not installed in the book’s environment, and the filtered readout was not tested with it. Those two library problems and the path to JAX are proposed at the end of the book, together with the new version of qang.

title: 20  Weight-conserving quantum neural networks (WeightQNN)
section: 20.8 The qg encoding and quantum signal processing
text:
20.8 The qg encoding and quantum signal processing
Encoding a feature \(x\in[-1,1]\) with \(\theta=\arccos x\) is the encoding of Chapter 1: the state has \(m_Z=1000\,x\), and the encoding angle is its qang angle (§16). Loaded \(L\) times, the model is a Chebyshev polynomial of degree \(L\) (\(\cos L\theta=T_L(x)\), checked to \(7\cdot10^{-16}\)), so \(L\) layers fit any bounded polynomial of degree \(L\) to machine precision and \(L-1\) layers do not. It is a polynomial inductive bias, not an advantage: with periodic targets angle encoding wins by 1.5 to 4.5 orders of magnitude.
The same rotation is the signal rotation of quantum signal processing (QSP), and qang.qsp builds it in qg terms (§134). As activations of a one-layer Kolmogorov–Arnold network, weighted QSP gets 179 of 189 inputs right, 182 with odd and even activations, against 185 for qang’s network E (§135–§136): the limit is the parity of the activations, not the number of phases.

title: 20  Weight-conserving quantum neural networks (WeightQNN)
text:
20.12 Summary

In the weight-1 sector the network is an orthogonal matrix and each qubit reads \(m_Z=1000(1-2u_q^2)\). Under equal T1 the qg filter returns the noiseless readout exactly, at a cost \(K=(1-\gamma)^{kd}\) known before running; without it, the readings drift towards the north pole.
Trained on a simulator, the network gains 2.5 points with qang at weight 1 and 16.5 at weight 2; trained under the calibrated noise, it gains nothing measurable. The filter does not correct unequal T1 or dephasing.
Weight 2 reaches weight 1 with an encoding that does not distort and a full-rank readout (\(qg_{ZZ}\)).
The network is a simulable quadratic classifier: robustness on noisy hardware, not quantum advantage.
In PennyLane the filtered gradient under T1 is the noiseless one; the check turned up two library problems (PennyLane and qiskit-machine-learning) and a path to JAX, which are proposed at the end of the book.

title: 21  The qg symmetry filter and exactness under T1 relaxation
text:
21.1 From the base: decay pushes the readings to the north pole
Chapter 20 used the qg filter as a tool: discarding the shots that left the Hamming-weight sector returns the noiseless readout under T1. This chapter treats it as an object. First the theorem and why it holds, on the scale of Chapter 1. Then what it costs, with a closed rule that predicts before running when it pays, and what it does not correct: unequal T1 across qubits, dephasing, and gate and readout errors. For each limit there is an exact property (F5 and F6 in the notes) that says how to go on. The structural facts are checked with code on random states; the classification results are those of the notes, with predictions committed before running.
Amplitude damping of one qubit has two Kraus operators:
\[
K_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\end{pmatrix},\qquad K_1=\sqrt\gamma\,|0\rangle\langle1|.
\]
\(K_1\) is the jump: the qubit falls to \(|0\rangle\), and its reading goes to \(+1000\) m-qg, the north pole. \(K_0\) is the no-jump evolution: it leaves \(|0\rangle\) alone and multiplies the amplitude of \(|1\rangle\) by \(\sqrt{1-\gamma}\). In a register, the product of the \(K_0\) multiplies every basis state with \(k\) ones by \((1-\gamma)^{k/2}\), the same factor for every state of the weight-\(k\) sector. And any jump lowers the weight by one.
Hence the theorem (notes, §77 and §78 F4): with the same T1 on every qubit, keeping the weight-\(k\) shots returns the noiseless state. The no-jump factor is a scalar on the sector, and it disappears on normalising; everything that jumped is in another sector. It holds between layers of weight-conserving gates, for any strength and any depth. The fraction of shots that survives is \(K=(1-\gamma)^{k\,d}\), with \(d\) the number of damping steps.
For a weight-2 state with three damping steps, the fraction left in the sector is 0.606355, exactly \(0.92^6\). The filter is a postselection, and what it returns is a conditional probability: the equation of Chapter 1 applied inside the sector.

21.2 What it costs: the mean-squared-error rule
The filter removes the bias and pays in shots: of \(S\) shots only \(KS\) remain. The notes (§94) wrote down before running a closed rule for the mean squared error of the qubits’ readings \(m\):
\[
\text{MSE}_{\text{qang}}\approx\frac{1000^2-m^2}{KS},\qquad
\text{MSE}_{\text{raw}}=\text{bias}^2+\frac{1000^2-m_{\text{raw}}^2}{S}.
\]
The first is the shot noise of Chapter 1 with \(KS\) shots; the second adds the bias towards the north pole, which does not shrink with more shots. The chapter’s script checks it with 10 random circuits of 6 qubits, weight 2, 12 sublayers and \(\gamma=0.02\) (\(K=0.616\)), 200 repetitions per point:

The raw error stalls at about 31,000 m-qg² (a bias of about 175 m-qg), while the filtered one keeps falling as \(1/S\). Setting the two expressions equal gives the break-even number of shots \(S^*\): above it, the filter wins. For the circuits of this chapter \(S^*\) runs from 9 to 61 shots (Figure 21.2, left); on the notes’ grid, from 3 to 110 (108 configurations up to 8 qubits, weight 4 and depth 24, with up to 1000 times less error with the filter).
With very few shots kept (§96, 405 configurations with \(K\) down to \(2.6\cdot10^{-7}\)) the generalised rule, which includes the bias left in the filtered readout, picks the winner in 342 of 342 cases with \(KS\ge5\), also with unequal T1 and dephasing. When less than one shot survives, the filter returns 0 for lack of data, and even so it beats the raw readout in 51 of 57 cases, because the raw one collapsed towards \(|0\dots0\rangle\), the north pole, which is a worse guess than the equator. No regime was found where the shot cost decides against the filter.

section: 21.4 F5: unequal T1 depends only on the ratios
text:
21.4 F5: unequal T1 depends only on the ratios
With a different T1 on each qubit, the no-jump factor is no longer a scalar on the sector: it is the product of the \(\sqrt{1-\gamma_q}\) of the excited qubits, different for each state. The filter then leaves a bias: 100 to 160 m-qg with a ±50% spread of the \(\gamma_q\) (Figure 21.1). But the notes found an exact property (§117 F5): a common factor in all the \((1-\gamma_q)\) cancels on normalising, so the filtered readout depends only on the ratios \((1-\gamma_q)/(1-\gamma_r)\). The script checks it by multiplying all the \((1-\gamma_q)\) by 0.85: the filtered readout moves by no more than \(10^{-12}\) m-qg in any sector, and the raw one moves by 640 to 850 m-qg.
The practical consequence is a recipe. Training with the filter under the calibrated rates needs only the relative T1s, tolerates calibration errors and survives a common drift of all the T1s:

section: 21.5 F6: dephasing, with the filter and extrapolation
text:
21.5 F6: dephasing, with the filter and extrapolation
Dephasing does not change the weight, so the filter does not see it. But the notes proved another exact property (§118 F6): with equal T1 and dephasing, the filtered readout is the readout with dephasing alone. The no-jump factor is a scalar on the sector and commutes with the dephasing channel, which is diagonal. The script checks it in every sector of 6 qubits, to \(7\cdot10^{-13}\) m-qg (Figure 21.1). The filter turns two noises into one, and that one can be extrapolated to zero (ZNE):

In the notes’ classifiers (§118, §122, at 5 and 8 qubits) linear extrapolation leaves 50–58% of the error of the filtered readings and Richardson 26–35%; without the filter, ZNE must extrapolate T1 and dephasing together and ends 3 to 10 points behind. With 1000 shots per scale, at weight 2, ZNE loses to the filter alone, because its shot cost eats the gain. What corrects dephasing best in a classifier is something else: training with the filter under the calibrated noise, which recovers the noiseless accuracy (0.951–0.963).
One subtlety (§132–§133): dephasing between RBS gates commutes with the weight and the filter does not see it, but dephasing inside the decomposition of an RBS into native gates turns a phase error into a change of weight. To predict the kept fraction on a device, the simulator has to place that error inside each RBS.

—
the simulator predicts \(K\) within 0.006 (ECR)
in favour as a prediction; the filter does not correct them






Balance. The filter is symmetry postselection, a known mitigation technique. What the notes add are the exact properties (the theorem in every sector, F5 and F6), the closed cost rule, and the recipe for each noise the filter does not correct. The base of Chapter 1 gives the picture: the jump takes the readings to the north pole, and the filter returns the conditional probability on the sector. When the noise is not equal T1, the filter alone is no longer enough, and the answer is to train with it under the calibrated noise.

21.9 In code
import numpy as np
from qang import qml as QML

m = QML.WeightQNN(n_qubits=6, weight=3, layers=2)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

21  The qg symmetry filter and exactness under T1 relaxation

title: 21  The qg symmetry filter and exactness under T1 relaxation
text:
21.10 Summary

The jump takes the readings to the north pole and lowers the weight; the no-jump evolution multiplies every weight-\(k\) state by \((1-\gamma)^{k/2}\). With equal T1, the filter returns the noiseless state in every sector, with \(K=(1-\gamma)^{kd}\).
The rule \(\text{MSE}\approx(1000^2-m^2)/(KS)\) against bias\(^2+(1000^2-m^2)/S\) predicts before running when filtering pays; the break-even is at a few tens of shots, and the cost never decided against it.
With unequal T1 the filtered readout depends only on the ratios of the rates (F5): training with the filter under the calibrated rates recovers the accuracy and withstands a common drift.
With T1 plus dephasing the filter leaves dephasing only (F6), which is extrapolated to zero or, in a classifier, corrected by training with the filter under the noise.
With gate and readout errors, qang’s simulator predicts a device’s kept fraction; the filter does not correct them.

21  The qg symmetry filter and exactness under T1 relaxation

title: 22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)
text:
22.1 From the base: two errors the filter treats differently
The qg filter of Chapter 21 makes the readout exact under equal T1, but it does not correct everything. Two things remain, and this chapter deals with them. The first are errors that conserve the weight and move the excitation from one qubit to another: they pass the filter, and must be measured separately, with echo circuits. The second is what decayed shots do to a classifier without the filter: they do not add random noise, they pull every decision towards the same class. Both are read on the scale of Chapter 1, and for both the chapter checks the mechanism with code and quotes the notes’ results on device noise models, with predictions committed before running.
In the weight-1 sector, each qubit reads \(m_Z(q)=1000(1-2p_q)\), with \(p_q\) the probability that the excitation is on it. There are two ways to go wrong:
The first is corrected by discarding; the second, by inverting \(M\), as a readout confusion matrix is inverted.
crumbs: VII. Quantum machine learning (QML) and the symmetry filter
22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)

title: 22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)
text:
A T1 jump takes the shot out of the sector: the excitation disappears and every qubit reads \(+1000\), the north pole. The filter discards those shots. Without the filter, the raw readout is a mixture: with probability \(K\) the noiseless readout, and with probability \(1-K\) the north pole on every qubit.
An in-sector error moves the excitation from one qubit to another: the shot still has weight 1, passes the filter and changes the readings of two qubits at once. On the probabilities \(p_q\) it acts as a stochastic matrix \(M\).

22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)

title: 22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)
text:
22.2 In-sector errors and the echo
An echo circuit prepares a basis state of the sector, \(|e_j\rangle\), applies the network’s gates and then their inverses. Without errors it returns to \(|e_j\rangle\); with errors, its filtered distribution over the sector states is column \(j\) of a transfer matrix \(M\) (notes, §105). Since the real circuit has half the echo’s gates, the correction uses \(M^{1/2}\): the filtered distribution \(f\) is unmixed by solving \(M^{1/2}x=f\) with \(x\ge0\) (qang.sectors.unmix_sector).

section: 22.4 The pull: why the loss without qang varies between seeds
text:
22.4 The pull: why the loss without qang varies between seeds
In the multiclass network of Chapter 20, the loss without the filter varied a lot from one seed to another (from −0.7 to 41.7 points). The notes explained it with an exact property (§121 F7). At weight 1 under equal T1, every decayed shot lands in \(|0\dots0\rangle\), where each qubit reads \(+1000\). Since the logits are linear in the readings, the raw logits are
\[
\text{logits}_{\text{raw}}=K\,L+(1-K)\,v,
\]
with \(L\) the noiseless logits and \(v\) the logits of the north pole, a constant vector fixed by training (for the linear head, \(v=W^\top\mathbf 1+b\)). Without the filter, every input is pulled towards the class with the largest \(v_c\), and how much that weighs is measured by a pull index: \((1-K)/K\) times the range of \(v\), over the median training margin.
The script checks it on 40 five-class models with random parameters (\(K=0.472\), 300 inputs each):

the formula for the raw logits holds to \(7\cdot10^{-15}\);
without the filter, 0 to 60% of the decisions flip depending on the model, and the flips grow with the pull index (Spearman 0.60; in the notes, 0.65 with the head and 0.98 with the qubit readout);
with the filter, none flips.

The spread between seeds is not bad luck: it is the \(v\) that training left, and it can be read before running anything.






Figure 22.2: Fraction of decisions that flip without the filter against the pull index, for 40 five-class models under equal T1. With biases (standard readout), the flips grow with the pull; the pull-free readout flips none.

title: 22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)
text:
22.5 The pull-free readout
If the pull comes from \(v\), it can be removed by design: logits linear in the excitation probabilities with no constant term (for the head, \(W^\top(qg_Z-1)\); for the qubit readout, \(a\,p_c\)). Then the north pole contributes zero, decayed shots only rescale the logits by \(K\), and the raw decision is the noiseless one. The script checks it on the 40 models: no decision flips, and the raw logits are \(K\) times the noiseless ones to \(6\cdot10^{-15}\). title: 22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)
text:
22.6 Calibrating with the device itself
The notes tried two more ways of using calibration on IBM noise models (§119, §120): training with qang under the published T1 and T2, and measuring the device itself (with the echo matrix inside the model, or refitting the readout on 40 inputs run on the device). None beat the simple recipe: train noiseless and run with the filter (0.972 mean accuracy against 0.979 noiseless), plus the echo for the decision values. The reason is that gate errors dominate on those models, and a T1/T2 calibration does not describe them (the per-sublayer \(\gamma\) are only 0.002–0.017).

title: 22  Echo calibration and the noise bias (pull effect)
text:
22.10 Summary

A T1 jump takes every qubit to the north pole and the shot out of the sector; an in-sector error moves the excitation and passes the filter. The first is discarded; the second is measured with echoes and inverted.
The echo with \(M^{1/2}\) removes more than half of the filtered error in the chapter’s model and 27–47% on the notes’ simulated devices; the full \(M\) over-corrects. It helps when the filtered error exceeds its shot noise.
Without the filter, the raw logits are exactly \(K\,L+(1-K)\,v\): decay pulls every decision towards one class, and the pull index predicts how much.
A bias-free readout makes the north pole worth zero: the raw decisions are the noiseless ones, without filtering and without losing accuracy.
On IBM noise models, training noiseless and running with the filter (and the echo) was the best recipe; calibrating with the device did not improve it.

title: 23  Information geometry, the natural gradient (QNG) and kernels
text:
23.1 From the base: the angle and the readout
Chapters 20 to 22 read in qg what comes out of a circuit. This chapter asks about what goes in: the parameters an optimizer moves. An attractive idea circulates: if qg is the natural readout, writing the circuit in qg coordinates should speed up the gradient and flatten the landscape. The chapter shows with code that it is the other way round, and why. The coordinate to optimize in is the qang angle \(\theta\), and qg is the coordinate to read out in. Four honest uses of qang follow from that distinction: regularizing the pole singularity, reading the natural-gradient metric from qg correlators, damping the step near the poles, and writing a local cost that flattens more slowly. The structural results are checked with code; the kernel results on device noise models are the notes’, with predictions committed before running.
In Chapter 1, a qubit prepared with \(R_y(\theta)|0\rangle\) reads \(m_Z=1000\cos\theta\) m-qg, and \(\theta\) is the qang angle. Both coordinates describe the same state, but they are not equivalent for optimizing, because the change between them is not linear:
\[
\frac{d\,qg_Z}{d\theta}=-\sin\theta ,\qquad \frac{dE}{d\,qg_Z}=-\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\,\frac{dE}{d\theta}.
\]
At the poles (\(m_Z=\pm1000\)) the readout barely moves when \(\theta\) changes, and so the gradient in qg diverges. The whole chapter follows from that line.
crumbs: VII. Quantum machine learning (QML) and the symmetry filter
23  Information geometry, the natural gradient (QNG) and kernels

title: 23  Information geometry, the natural gradient (QNG) and kernels
text:
23.2 The singularity and its regularizations
The factor \(-1/\sin\theta\) is \(-10\) at \(\theta=0.1\), \(-100\) at \(0.01\) and \(-1000\) at \(0.001\). The notes (§1) propose two bounded versions, in qang.gradients:

clipping: \(-1/(\operatorname{sign}(\sin\theta)\max(|\sin\theta|,\varepsilon))\), never larger than \(1/\varepsilon\);
Tikhonov: \(-\sin\theta/(\sin^2\theta+\varepsilon^2)\), smooth everywhere and zero at the pole itself.

With \(\varepsilon=0.05\), at \(\theta=0.001\) the raw factor is 1000, the clipped one 20 and the Tikhonov one 0.40. title: 23  Information geometry, the natural gradient (QNG) and kernels
section: 23.3 The angle is the Fisher-flat coordinate
text:
23.3 The angle is the Fisher-flat coordinate
The underlying reason is statistical. Measuring in Z, the Fisher information per shot is (notes §15.1, §159)
\[
F_\theta=1, \qquad F_{qg}=\frac{1}{1-qg_Z^2}=\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}.
\]
In the angle it is 1 everywhere; in qg it depends on where one is and diverges at the poles. It is the same \(1/\sin\theta\) as in the previous section, now as the Fubini-Study metric written in qg coordinates. In Chapter 1 units, the standard deviation of the readout with \(N\) shots is \(\sigma_m=1000\sin\theta/\sqrt N\) m-qg (the sample mean attains the Cramér-Rao bound), and that of the estimated angle is \(1/\sqrt N\) radians, the same all around the circle.
The script checks it with 4000 repetitions of 1000 shots at 12 angles: \(\sigma_{qg}\sqrt N\) reproduces \(\sin\theta\) to the third digit (0.149 against 0.149 at \(\theta=0.15\); 0.995 against 0.992 at \(1.70\)), and \(\sigma_\theta\sqrt N\) stays between 0.98 and 1.05 at every point (Figure 23.1, left). The angle is the flat coordinate: in it, each optimizer step is worth the same anywhere.
A coordinate does not save evaluations. For a gate \(e^{-i\theta G}\) with \(G^2=I/4\), the energy is \(E(\theta)=a+b\cos\theta+c\sin\theta\). A single shifted evaluation is not enough for the derivative: the script builds two functions of that form that agree at \(\theta+\pi/2\) (both \(-0.644218\)) and have different derivatives at \(\theta\) (\(-0.644\) and \(+0.765\)). Two evaluations suffice, so two per parameter is the minimum in any coordinate. In qg the same two numbers are used and the pole is added.






Figure 23.1: Left: standard deviation times \(\sqrt N\) of the readout in m-qg (divided by 1000) and of the estimated angle, with 1000 shots; the readout follows \(\sin\theta\) and the angle stays at 1. Right: descent from the pole on \(E=-\sin\theta\); in raw qg the optimizer jumps between the poles, and the regularized versions converge more slowly than in \(\theta\).

title: 23  Information geometry, the natural gradient (QNG) and kernels
section: 23.4 The natural gradient and the qg_YY metric
text:
23.4 The natural gradient and the qg_YY metric
The natural gradient (QNG, Stokes et al., 2020) corrects the step with the metric: \(\Delta\theta=-\eta\,g^{-1}\nabla E\). For one qubit, the natural step in qg is exactly plain descent in \(\theta\) (notes §15.1): invariance under the change of coordinates means that writing it in qg adds nothing.
With several qubits there is something qang does contribute (§159). In a real ansatz of \(R_y\) and CZ, every state along the circuit is real, so \(\langle Y_k\rangle=0\) before every \(R_y\) and every diagonal entry of the metric is exactly 1/4. The angles are flat one by one, and all the curvature sits off the diagonal. Within a layer those terms are \(g_{ij}=\langle Y_iY_j\rangle/4\): qg_YY correlators read from one Y-basis circuit per layer. It is the block-diagonal metric of Stokes et al. written as qg readouts. The script checks it on the 4-qubit TFIM with 3 layers: the diagonal is 1/4 to \(1.7\cdot10^{-16}\), the qg_YY blocks match the full metric within each layer to \(1.7\cdot10^{-16}\), and off the diagonal there are entries up to 0.248, which is where the metric acts.
The notes’ experiment, with predictions committed before running: 4-qubit TFIM (\(h=1\)), 12 parameters, success if \(E-E_0\le0.03\) within 300 steps (the ansatz floor is 0.0245), rate chosen on 6 seeds and 20 test seeds. title: 23  Information geometry, the natural gradient (QNG) and kernels
text:
23.5 Pole-damped descent
If the problem is at the poles, one can brake there without leaving the angle (notes §9):
\[
\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\max(|\sin\theta|,\varepsilon)\,\frac{dE}{d\theta}.
\]
The factor is \(|d\,qg_Z/d\theta|\), the same geometry as in the first section, and it needs no tuning. It is the natural step multiplied by \(|\sin\theta|\), which for these real states is also the coherence \(2|\rho_{01}|\): the optimizer slows down the less coherence the qubit has left. It is not a new class of optimizer: it is a position-dependent step, of the trust-region kind.

The figures differ somewhat from the notes’ (§9.2): there, at rate 0.3, the damped version lost a few points (0.963 against 0.997), and the gains from rate 2 were 2.5 to 5 times. The pattern is the same; the exact figures depend on the landscapes drawn.

23.6 Quantum kernels and the qg filter
A fidelity kernel \(K_{ij}=|\langle\psi(x_i)|\psi(x_j)\rangle|^2\) estimated on a noisy device comes out shrunk (\(K_{ii}<1\)) and pulled towards the noise value. The usual repair, \(K_{ij}/\sqrt{K_{ii}K_{jj}}\), costs the diagonal circuits. If the kernel circuit conserves the Hamming weight, the qg filter of Chapter 21 is another repair (notes §161). With the weight-1 encoding (one qubit per component of the normalized vector), the kernel is \(K=(x\cdot y)^2\), and in qg it is a qang angle: \(\arccos(2K-1)=2\varphi\), with \(\varphi\) the angle between the two vectors. The script checks it to \(1.3\cdot10^{-15}\).
The notes’ experiment: breast-cancer data reduced to 4 components plus a constant (5 qubits), 40 + 40 points, SVM with a precomputed kernel, 2000 shots and three IBM device noise models.

23.7 Barren plateaus: global cost against the qg local cost
With many qubits, the gradient of a random circuit becomes exponentially small (McClean et al., 2018). The notes looked at it in qg twice. In §12, converting the gradient to qg changes nothing: the plateau stays exponential, regularization only rescales it, and at the poles the singularity is added on top. The two are independent and compound.
In §23 the coordinate does matter, by another route: the cost. An ansatz is trained to reach a product state, and two costs that vanish only at the target are compared: the global one, \(C_G=1-P(0\dots0)\), and the local one of Cerezo et al. (2021), which on the Chapter 1 scale is the register’s mean readout, \(C_L=(1-\overline{qg_Z})/2\). With short circuits (\(L=2\)), the qg local cost decays like a polynomial and the global one like an exponential: at \(n=10\) the local one has 470 times more variance (in the notes, 5600 times at \(n=12\)), that is, about 470 times fewer shots for the same signal-to-noise ratio.
With deep circuits (\(L=4n\)) the local cost does not cure the plateau: both decay exponentially.
With finite shots (notes §23, 100 shots per circuit), the global gradient comes out exactly zero in 22% of the initialisations at \(n=10\) and 35% at \(n=12\); the local one, never. Training at \(n=10\), the local cost reaches fidelity 0.5 in a median of 11 steps against 20 for the global one.
The classical control. With depth \(L\), each \(\langle Z_i\rangle\) depends only on the \(2L+1\) qubits in its light cone, so the local cost and its gradient are computed classically in time \(O(n\,2^{2L+1})\). The notes train 50 and 100 qubits that way, without shots. Where the qg local cost escapes the plateau it is also simulable: the advantage is in training, not quantum.

title: 23  Information geometry, the natural gradient (QNG) and kernels
text:
23.11 Summary

On the Chapter 1 scale, \(dE/d\,qg_Z=-(1/\sin\theta)\,dE/d\theta\) diverges at the poles. Raw descent in qg jumps from pole to pole; clipping and Tikhonov fix it, but converge more slowly than descent in \(\theta\).
The Fisher information is 1 in the angle and \(1/(1-qg_Z^2)\) in qg: the qang angle is the flat coordinate. Optimize in \(\theta\) and read out in qg, with \(\sigma_m=1000\sin\theta/\sqrt N\) m-qg.
No change of coordinate goes below two evaluations per parameter.
In a real ansatz the metric’s diagonal is exactly 1/4 and the blocks are qg_YY correlators. The block metric helps a little (1.3 times); the full one, 4.6 times; counting circuits, the three methods end within 15%.
Damping by \(|\sin\theta|\) is not a new optimizer, but it withstands aggressive rates when starting near a pole.
The qg filter repairs the Gram matrix of a fixed-weight kernel better than the normalization and without its circuits; accuracy barely changes.
The qg local cost escapes the plateau only with short circuits, and there it is also classically simulable.

title: 24  Hamiltonian simulation, quantum walks and VarQTE
text:
24.1 From the base: conserving N means having a filter
Simulating the time evolution of a quantum system is the most natural application of a quantum computer, and it is also where the qg filter of Chapter 21 reaches furthest: many Hamiltonians of physics conserve the number of excitations, and so do their Trotter circuits. Then the Hamming weight of each shot is a free witness, and the filter applies to every observable read in Z. This chapter goes through time evolution on the Chapter 1 scale: XY and XXZ chains, a quantum walk, noise channels as maps of the readouts, variational evolution at fixed depth and, more briefly, differential equations, Hubbard, a gauge theory, coherence in Ising and Boltzmann machines. The structural results are checked with code; the results on device noise models are those of the notes’ committed runs, read from their stored files.
On the Chapter 1 scale, each qubit reads \(m_Z=1000(1-2p)\), with \(p\) the probability that it is excited. The number of excitations of a shot is its Hamming weight, and the register’s mean readout counts it: \(N=\sum_i(1-qg_{Z,i})/2\). If the Hamiltonian conserves \(N\) and so does every gate of the circuit, every shot with the wrong weight had an error, and the filter discards it (Chapter 21).
With a single excitation, the state lives in \(n\) amplitudes, one per qubit: the excitation hops between neighbouring qubits. It is a continuous-time quantum walk, and each qubit’s readout says where the walker is.

section: 24.2 Trotter and the quantum walk on the XY chain
text:
24.2 Trotter and the quantum walk on the XY chain
The XY chain with fields, \(H=J\sum_k(X_kX_{k+1}+Y_kY_{k+1})/2+\sum_kh_kZ_k/2\), conserves \(N\), and its first-order Trotter circuit uses only \(R_Z\) and XX+YY gates, which conserve it too (notes, §147).
How many steps. More Trotter steps lower the Trotter error and add noise, so on a device the error has a minimum at a number of steps \(r^*\). Noiselessly, with \(n=5\), random fields and \(T=3\), the script recomputes the Trotter error: 0.381, 0.363, 0.221, 0.140, 0.078, 0.054 and 0.033 with 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 steps. On the notes’ 21 IBM device noise models, the filter (plus readout correction) halved the best error (median 0.147 → 0.067; 1.6 to 2.8 times depending on the device) and moved \(r^*\) from 8 to 12 steps in the median: the filter lets the simulation use deeper circuits. On 11 devices the optimum was 12, the deepest tested.
The walk. With \(n=7\) and the walker in the middle, the variance of its position \(\sigma^2(t)\) grows like \(t^2\) in a quantum (ballistic) walk and like \(t\) in a classical (diffusive) one. The script computes it with the exact evolution in the weight-1 sector:

T1 leaks through the CNOTs. Each decay lowers \(N\), and the filter catches it if the state is in the sector when it happens. Inside a three-CNOT bond the intermediate states are not in the sector, and a decay mid-gate can be rotated back to \(N=n/2\) and pass. With gates that conserve \(N\) at every point, the filter removes 99.5%.
Z dephasing does not change \(N\), and the filter does not see it.
With mixed noise, filter plus ZNE sits 2.6 to 8 times below the best single method up to 4 steps (§60).

On the 21 simulated IBM devices with \(n=6\) (§148), the filter’s gain falls from 5.6 times with one excitation to 2.6 with two and with three: sectors with more excitations keep more shots, but more of the noise lands inside them. The prediction that the filter never makes things worse failed in one of 63 cases (FakeKyoto at half filling). On IonQ’s forte-1 noise model (§61), the filter removed about half of the error in both XY compilations, with a ratio of 0.82 between them, inside the committed band: on trapped ions, without dominant T1, the CNOT leak does not appear.

24.5 Variational evolution at fixed depth
Trotter grows with time: more time, more steps, more gates. Variational evolution (VarQTE, McLachlan’s principle) fixes the circuit and changes only its angles (notes §162). title: 24  Hamiltonian simulation, quantum walks and VarQTE
text:
24.6 Differential equations
A one-qubit re-uploading circuit can solve a differential equation: \(u(x)=u_0+s(f(x)-f(0))\) with \(f=\langle Z\rangle\), trained on the residual (notes §22). The qang question is how to encode \(x\): in the angle, or with \(\arccos\), so that \(x\) is a qg readout. The notes’ result: qg wins clearly on exponential decay (2.3, 17 and 6.6 times better than the best angle scale with 2, 3 and 4 layers) and does not win in general: on the logistic equation the angle is about 2 times better, and on the sine 25 times. qg has no scale to tune; the angle does (with scale \(\pi\) it fails everywhere). The classical control, Chebyshev collocation with as many coefficients as parameters, solves everything to \(10^{-7}\) or better. The result says which encoding to use, not that the circuit beats a classical method.

section: 24.7 Hubbard and a gauge theory: symmetry filters on every observable
text:
24.7 Hubbard and a gauge theory: symmetry filters on every observable
1D Hubbard (notes §29): 4 sites on 8 qubits, one register per spin. The Hamiltonian conserves \(N_\uparrow\) and \(N_\downarrow\), so each register has zero mean readout at all times, and every observable (charge imbalance, double occupancy) is in Z. The script checks it noiselessly: mean readout 0 in both registers and kept fraction 1 at 1, 2, 4 and 8 steps. In the notes, the filters roughly halve the error on a device without routing, and ZNE plus spin filters gives the best double occupancy (6 to 9 times below raw). On the heavy-hex lattice, routing creates spin leak (8 to 47% of the right-\(N\) shots land in the wrong spin sector), and there the second filter pays. From 4 steps on everything sits on the noise floor.
\(\mathbb Z_2\) lattice gauge theory (§66): 4 matter sites and 3 links. The Gauss law \(G_j\) is a product of Z’s, so it is the qg readout of a parity: the same Z shots give the local Gauss witnesses and three filters (\(N\), Gauss and both). The script checks that noiselessly each \(\langle G_j\rangle\) is exactly \(\pm1\) and no shot is lost. In the notes, with 2 steps, the Gauss filter removes more than the \(N\) filter (80 against 64% under depolarizing noise) and both together 90%. Under T1, 58–65%: the same CNOT leak. The local witnesses do not locate errors in this homogeneous model. Gauss-law post-selection is known; what qang adds is reading it as qg of parities from the same shots.

section: 24.8 Coherence in the transverse-field Ising model
text:
24.8 Coherence in the transverse-field Ising model
The difference between the Z-basis entropy and the entropy of the state is a known measure: the relative entropy of coherence \(C(\rho)\) (Baumgratz, Cramer and Plenio, 2014). It needs the entropy of the state, which counts do not give. The notes (§34) propose a bound from two readouts per qubit:
\[
C\geq\sum_i\left[qg_S(qg_{Z,i})-qg_S(|r_i|)\right],\qquad |r_i|=\sqrt{qg_{X,i}^2+qg_{Y,i}^2+qg_{Z,i}^2}.
\]
The script evaluates it on thermal states of the 6-qubit Ising ring at 20 points (\(\beta\) from 0.25 to 3, field \(g\) from 0.25 to 2): it captures 92.3 to 99.8% of the coherence (Figure 24.2, right). The single-qubit bound captures 15–17% (1/6 of the sum, by symmetry), and the basis-entropy bound is useless: it goes down to −5.9 bits. With 1000 shots the bound reads to ±0.04 bits. Where it fails: on a graph state every reduced qubit is \(I/2\) and the bound gives 0 with \(C=6\) bits. The tightness is a property of these thermal states, not a law.






Figure 24.2: Left: share of the imbalance error the filter removes on the XXZ chain, one noise source at a time; under T1 the CNOTs let half through and N-conserving gates almost nothing. Right: share of the coherence of Ising thermal states captured by the qg bound.

title: 24  Hamiltonian simulation, quantum walks and VarQTE
text:
24.9 Boltzmann machines: the I–η plane
A recent review (Singh et al., 2026) looks at each visible–hidden pair of an RBM through two numbers: the covariance \(\eta\) and the mutual information \(I\), which lie between two bounds \(LB(\eta)\) and \(UB(\eta)\), and observes that trained RBMs sit on \(LB\). In qg (notes §47), a pair of spins is fixed by three numbers, \(qg_v\), \(qg_h\) and \(\eta\), and the script checks: \(LB\) is exactly the case of zero marginals (\(2.2\cdot10^{-16}\)) and the minimum of \(I\) at fixed \(\eta\); \(UB\) is the locked pair with \(|qg_v|=|qg_h|=\sqrt{1-\eta}\) (\(2.9\cdot10^{-15}\)). In between, to leading order, \(I-LB\approx\eta^2(qg_v^2+qg_h^2)/(2\ln2)\); with \(\eta=0.2\)–\(0.4\) the formula sits 10–14% above the exact value, because it is leading order in \(\eta\) too.
The explanation: the Ising driver has \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry, a symmetric RBM has zero marginals, and so it sits on \(LB\) by symmetry, not by a learning principle. The prediction, which could have failed, held: a longitudinal field moves the same learner off \(LB\) by the amount the marginals set.

The gains that depend on the scale itself (the ODE) are partial, and the chapter says so.

title: 24  Hamiltonian simulation, quantum walks and VarQTE
text:
24.13 Summary

If the Hamiltonian and the gates conserve \(N\), each shot’s weight is a witness and the filter reaches every Z observable.
On the XY chain, the filter halves the best error and moves the Trotter optimum to deeper circuits; the raw walk looks classical (exponent 0.87) and the filtered one is ballistic (1.84; exact 1.96).
Under T1, CNOTs let half the error through and N-conserving gates almost none (99.5% removed).
Every channel is an affine map of the readouts; fixed-depth VarQTE wins at late times.
Differential equations, Hubbard, gauge, coherence in Ising and RBMs: the filter and the qg readouts help where the chapter measures it, and where they do not, it says so.

title: 25  Quantum spectroscopy, PCA and molecular chemistry
text:
25.1 From the base: counting electrons with the register readout
Chapter 24 used the conservation of the number of excitations to filter dynamics. This one does the same with spectra and molecules, where the conserved number is the number of electrons. The register’s mean readout, on the Chapter 1 scale, counts the electrons of each shot; if the circuit conserves them, that number is both a reference-free error witness and a filter. The chapter follows that idea from a data PCA to 12-qubit molecules, and also shows where it stops reaching: when the error lives in terms that are not measured in Z. The structural results are checked with code; the noise-model results are those of the notes’ committed runs.
In the Jordan-Wigner encoding each qubit is a spin-orbital, and its occupation is \((1-qg_Z)/2\), that is \((1000-m_Z)/2000\) in m-qg. Summing over the register,
\[
N_e=\sum_i\frac{1-qg_{Z,i}}{2},\qquad \overline{qg_Z}=1-\frac{2N_e}{n}.
\]
For any circuit that conserves the number of electrons, the ideal mean readout is known before running (0 for H\(_2\): 2 electrons on 4 qubits). A departure from it is a witness that the hardware added or removed electrons (T1 pushes it towards \(+1\)), and shot by shot it is a filter. The filter is the known symmetry verification (Bonet-Monroig et al., 2018; McArdle et al., 2019); what qang adds is the witness and its reading.
crumbs: VIII. Many-body dynamics, open channels, matter and chemistry
25  Quantum spectroscopy, PCA and molecular chemistry

title: 25  Quantum spectroscopy, PCA and molecular chemistry
text:
25.2 PCA in the weight-1 sector
Quantum PCA diagonalizes \(\rho=C/\mathrm{tr}\,C\). In the unary encoding, a mixture of the loaded data vectors (with weights \(|x_j|^2\)) is exactly that \(\rho\), and an RBS circuit applying the PCA rotation leaves eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\) on qubit \(k\) (notes §146). The script checks it with exact states: for 5 components and 16 data points, each qubit’s excitation probability is the normalized eigenvalue (0.640, 0.203, 0.122, 0.023, 0.011) to \(2.2\cdot10^{-16}\), with 10 RBS in the rotation. Every gate conserves the weight, so the filter applies. It is not the quantum-PCA speed-up (5 components use 5 qubits and the rotation is computed classically): it tests how well a device reads a known spectrum.
On the notes’ 21 IBM device noise models, with all four committed predictions passing, the raw estimate is biased upwards: shots leaving the sector add excitations on every qubit (median L1 error 0.266). Filter plus readout correction brings it to 0.048 (4.6 times lower; 1.6 to 7.7 depending on the device) and orders all five eigenvalues correctly on 18 of 21 devices (raw: 13). What is left is a flattening of the spectrum that grows when few shots are kept (FakeKyoto keeps 15% and fails).

25.3 H\(_2\): the witness and the filter
The script checks the structure on the notes’ H\(_2\) Hamiltonian (STO-3G, 0.735 Å, 4 qubits): it commutes exactly with \(N\), \(N_\uparrow\) and \(N_\downarrow\); the \(N\)-conserving ansatz reaches the exact (FCI) energy to \(5\cdot10^{-11}\) mHa, and the register’s ideal mean readout is 0. Hartree-Fock sits 20.3 mHa above. The notes (§21) ran fake brisbane’s noise model with 20,000 shots and an idle delay before measurement that amplifies T1:

The witness rises as electrons are lost. With the filter the energy is 3.2 times better than with readout correction alone without delay (6 times at 50 µs) and 3.7 times better than Hartree-Fock, but still 3.4 times above chemical accuracy: the rest sits in the 4 XXYY-type terms, which a Z filter cannot reach, and in errors that conserve \(N\). Spin filters (§28). The Hamiltonian conserves \(N_\uparrow\) and \(N_\downarrow\) separately, and each spin register has its own mean readout. A second free filter, from the same shots: under depolarizing noise it removes a further 34–37% of the error the total filter leaves, but on fake brisbane the gain is within the seed spread (6.5 → 5.9 mHa), because the spin leak is below 1%. The leak witness says when it pays.

title: 25  Quantum spectroscopy, PCA and molecular chemistry
text:
25.5 Checks that reach every group
If the problem is reach, the remedy is a check that commutes with every term (§52): the parity of the electron number on an ancilla (6 CNOTs), and \(N\) modulo 4 on a second ancilla, which also catches the errors that change \(N\) by 2. With 3-layer LiH and all-to-all noise, parity plus mod 4 take the error from 83.9 to 13.4 mHa (§50’s best was 76.6), discarding 28% of the shots: for the first time in the repository, LiH ends (on that model) below Hartree-Fock. On IonQ’s forte-1 model (§53) the mod-4 check survives (3.8 times less error, parity alone 1.25 times), but the result stays above Hartree-Fock.

Number checks keep working up to 12 qubits, but they reach a shrinking share of the error: the part that changes \(N\) falls from 92% (LiH, 60 CX) to 67% (H\(_6\), 132 CX). The rest conserves \(N\) and no number check sees it.
Splitting by spin recovers part of it (from 75.7 to 66.8 mHa on H\(_4\)).
The projection onto the singlet \(S^2=0\) removes a further 37–38%, the largest gain since §52, but \(S^2\) is not diagonal in Z: it needs 640 Pauli strings for the projector and 2064–3456 for the projector times \(H\), against 105–185 for \(H\).

Λ as a third filter (§153). A linear molecule conserves \(\Lambda\), the projection of the orbital angular momentum on its axis. With the π orbitals written as π± (\(m_l=\pm1\)), \(\Lambda\) is diagonal and is checked shot by shot with only the four π qubits, so it reaches 29 of LiH’s 317 measurement groups (10 qubits), against 1 for the number filter. The committed prediction half held: where \(N_\uparrow,N_\downarrow\) already applies, \(\Lambda\) adds almost nothing (13.9 → 13.3 mHa on FakeBrisbane), because changing \(\Lambda\) without changing \(N\) takes two errors. The extra reach is real and does not pay: in the 28 groups where only \(\Lambda\) acts, it discards 4–10% of the shots and their error barely moves, because the error that matters there is on the σ qubits measured in X/Y.

text:
25.7 Constrained optimization: QAOA with “exactly K”
Choosing exactly \(K\) of \(n\) vertices is the same identity as the number of electrons: \(\overline{qg_Z}=1-2K/n\), 0.25 for \(K=3\) of \(n=8\) (notes §30). The script checks that with the XY mixer (which conserves the weight, from a Dicke state) the ideal distribution is 100% feasible at random angles, while penalty QAOA leaves 10 to 45% feasible mass. On an all-to-all device the filter doubles the XY mixer’s probability of finding the optimum (0.150 → 0.278 at \(p=1\); 0.177 → 0.366 at \(p=2\)), and on the IonQ models too (1.8–2.6 times, §38). On fake brisbane, with routing, everything falls to the level of picking a random feasible set, and the kept fraction warns of it (0.24–0.33, close to 0.22 for a mixed register). Classical wins: a greedy algorithm reaches 98.5% of the optimum. The qg ingredients improve QAOA against QAOA, not against classical optimization.

title: 25  Quantum spectroscopy, PCA and molecular chemistry
text:
25.11 Summary

In Jordan-Wigner, the register’s mean readout counts the electrons: \(\overline{qg_Z}=1-2N_e/n\). Its ideal value is known before running, so it is a reference-free witness and, shot by shot, a filter.
In the unary PCA, the filter cuts the error of the read spectrum 4.6 times; on H\(_2\), the energy error 3.2 to 6 times.
On LiH the Z filter does not reach the error, which sits in the X/Y groups; ancilla checks (parity and \(N\) mod 4) do, and cut the error 6–8 times.
With larger molecules each symmetry reaches a smaller share of the error; \(S^2\) removes a further 37–38% at the cost of many more measurements, and \(\Lambda\) adds reach without lowering the error.
The filtered inversion test gives the absolute fidelity; the raw swap test does not. In constrained QAOA the filter doubles the XY mixer’s success, and a classical algorithm still wins.
